title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Compartment syndrome develops when intracompartmental tissue pressure surpasses the perfusion pressure of the arterial supply, leading to ischemia and potential irreversible injury to muscles and nerves. Although most frequently linked to acute trauma or overuse, the condition can also result from iatrogenic, vascular, infectious, or metabolic causes. The lower leg—particularly the anterior compartment—is most commonly affected, but the syndrome may occur in other sites such as the thigh, forearm, or hand. This course reviews the timely recognition of tibial anterior compartment syndrome and prompt interventions essential to prevent complications such as contracture, rhabdomyolysis, and amputation.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This course explores the pathophysiology, diagnosis, and management of both acute and chronic exertional compartment syndrome. Participants will gain an in-depth understanding of the key clinical findings, the interpretation of pressure measurements, and evidence-based decision-making for timely surgical or conservative interventions. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying tibial anterior compartment syndrome, performing the recommended evaluation, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach when managing this condition, ultimately improving patient safety, optimizing outcomes, and reducing long-term morbidity.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Introduction
content: Compartment syndrome occurs when the tissue pressure within a given compartment exceeds the perfusion pressure of the arterial supply, resulting in ischemia to the muscles and nerves of the compartment. The etiology is varied; however, most commonly, compartment syndrome is related to acute trauma or overuse syndrome. In the leg, this can occur in any of the 4 compartments: anterior, lateral, superficial posterior, or deep posterior (see Image .  Leg Compartments). Compartment syndrome can occur in other places in the body as well, including the thigh, foot, forearm, hand, and wrist.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Introduction
content: The muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg include the tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus, and peroneus tertius. In general, these muscles are responsible for ankle dorsiflexion and participate in eversion and inversion of the foot and ankle. More specifically, the tibialis anterior dorsiflexes and inverts the foot at the ankle joint. The extensor digitorum longus extends digits 2 to 5 and dorsiflexes the ankle, while the extensor hallucis longus is responsible for extension of the first digit. The extensor hallucis longus also dorsiflexes the ankle. The peroneus tertius aids in dorsiflexion and eversion. The leg's anterior compartment is supplied by the deep peroneal nerve (L4, L5, S1), which is a branch of the common peroneal nerve. Blood flow is supplied by the anterior tibial artery, which is a branch of the popliteal artery and transitions to the dorsalis pedis artery as it crosses into the foot. The borders of the anterior compartment are the anterior tibia, anteromedial fibula, interosseous membrane, and the anterior intermuscular septum.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Etiology
content: Trauma remains the most common cause of compartment syndrome, typically resulting from fractures, blunt or penetrating injuries, or associated hemorrhage. However, numerous nontraumatic etiologies have also been reported, including burns, infections (eg, tetanus or myositis), neurological events (eg, seizures), and toxic causes (eg, envenomation), prolonged drug or alcohol-induced coma, or anabolic steroid abuse. Additionally, renal derangements, particularly those leading to reduced serum osmolarity, may contribute to the development of compartment syndrome.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Etiology
content: Musculoskeletal causes of anterior tibial compartment syndrome include muscle tears within the anterior compartment, hypertrophy, or vigorous repetitive exercise, including both acute and chronic exertional forms. Chronic exertional compartment syndrome is a phenomenon caused by increased intracompartmental pressure during repetitive physical activity, leading to reduced blood flow and ischemia in the muscles, most commonly affecting the anterior compartment of the lower leg. Autoimmune and vascular conditions (eg, vasculitis, deep vein thrombosis, or hemorrhagic events) may also precipitate compartment syndrome. Additional causes include rhabdomyolysis and postischemic reperfusion swelling. [1]

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Etiology
content: Compartment syndrome may develop during routine medical or surgical care as a result of iatrogenic factors. Dressings, splints, or casts applied with excessive tightness can increase intracompartmental pressure and compromise perfusion. Prolonged placement in the lithotomy position can further elevate the risk by impairing venous outflow and promoting tissue swelling. Malfunctioning sequential compression devices may exert continuous pressure, contributing to compartmental hypertension. Intramuscular or intracompartmental injections, intraosseous lines, and the infusion of hypertonic intravenous fluid or contrast agents can increase compartment volume and pressure. Bleeding into the compartment following attempted cannulation of a vein or artery may also precipitate the condition. Additional contributing factors include the intraoperative use of pressurized pulsatile irrigation and the application of military antishock trousers, both of which can generate excessive external pressure. Orthopedic procedures can lead to compartment syndrome as well, often triggered by postoperative bleeding, muscle edema, or overly tight fascial closure following surgery.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Epidemiology
content: Tibial fracture represents the leading cause of acute compartment syndrome in the leg, accounting for up to 12% of all reported cases. Open tibial fractures contribute more frequently to the development of compartment syndrome (6%) than closed fractures (1.2%). Among patients with tibial diaphyseal fractures, younger individuals face a higher risk of developing the condition. [2] Greater fracture length relative to the total tibial length also correlates with increased risk. Tibial plateau fractures, particularly Schatzker VI types, carry a higher likelihood of compartment syndrome compared with shaft or pilon fractures. [3] [4] The presence of an accompanying fibular fracture further elevates the patient’s risk.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Epidemiology
content: Traumatic compartment syndrome tends to occur more often in men. Open fractures demonstrate a 2-fold increase in the likelihood of acute compartment syndrome. Complex fractures, substance use disorders, cirrhosis, and smoking each contribute additional risk factors for developing this condition. [5]

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Epidemiology
content: Chronic exertional compartment syndrome represents a relatively frequent source of leg pain in athletes, with an incidence ranging from 27% to 33%. Running athletes face the highest risk, and fascial defects appear in up to 40% of athletes compared with 5% in asymptomatic individuals. Symptoms commonly occur bilaterally, and both males and females are affected with equal frequency.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Epidemiology
content: In children, compartment syndrome without an associated fracture remains uncommon and poorly understood. The leg represents the most frequent site of involvement. A review of 39 pediatric cases identified vascular causes as the most prevalent etiology (28%), followed by trauma (26%), postoperative events (21%), exertion (15%), and infection (10%).

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: Compartment syndrome develops when increased pressure within a closed muscle compartment compromises perfusion. When systemic blood pressure cannot overcome intracompartmental pressure, ischemia of muscles, nerves, and other compartment contents occurs. [6] The condition may present as acute or chronic, depending on the underlying mechanism.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: Accumulation of fluid within a fixed-volume compartment, eg, from bleeding or soft tissue swelling, raises tissue and venous pressures. When interstitial pressure exceeds capillary perfusion pressure, capillaries collapse, reducing blood flow and causing tissue anoxia. [7] Muscle cells respond by releasing histamine-like substances that increase vascular permeability, drawing additional fluid into the compartment and worsening ischemia. As cellular lysis progresses, osmotic shifts further attract water from the vascular supply, amplifying pressure elevation. [8]

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: Tissue perfusion depends on the difference between systemic blood pressure and compartment pressure. Specifically, perfusion can be approximated by the equation: local blood flow (LBF) = [local arterial pressure – venous pressure] / local vascular resistance. Typically, the difference between diastolic blood pressure and compartment pressure exceeds 30 mm Hg, although some debate persists regarding this cutoff. Compartment pressures above 30 mm Hg warrant suspicion for compartment syndrome.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: Chronic exertional compartment syndrome results from reversible ischemia caused by repetitive physical activity, resolving with cessation of the triggering exercise. Rarely, continued activity may progress to irreversible acute compartment syndrome. Regular exercise can increase muscle volume by approximately 20%, and intramuscular pressure may remain elevated even after fasciotomy, suggesting additional pathophysiologic mechanisms. Contributing factors may include reduced capillary density, fewer capillaries, and abnormal arteriolar regulation, although the precise pathogenesis remains incompletely understood.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- History and Physical -- Clinical History
content: A thorough history plays a critical role in determining both the etiology and likelihood of compartment syndrome. Clinicians should review past medical and surgical history with attention to comorbidities that may influence presentation or management. In trauma cases, clarifying the mechanism of injury is essential, as high-velocity blunt trauma and penetrating injuries can precipitate compartment syndrome. [9] Medication history also provides important information, especially regarding the use of antiplatelet or anticoagulant agents, which may exacerbate bleeding and swelling. In nontraumatic presentations, history should explore potential toxicologic, iatrogenic, infectious, vascular, or systemic causes. Obtaining a reliable history may be particularly challenging in children or patients with multiple injuries due to limited cooperation or communication.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- History and Physical -- Clinical History
content: Patients classically present with pain that is disproportionate to physical findings, often described as deep, burning, aching, or as a sensation of fullness or tenseness within the limb. Neurologic symptoms, eg, paresthesias, numbness, tingling, or “pins and needles” commonly occur. Weakness may manifest as difficulty or inability to dorsiflex the foot or a subjective sense of the limb feeling “dead” or unusually weak.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
content: Examination should assess for skin breaks, swelling, erythema, discoloration, or other trauma signs. Palpation of the anterior compartment often reveals a firm, swollen, and tender muscle belly, typically in the middle to distal third of the leg. Pain usually worsens with passive stretching; in anterior compartment syndrome, passive plantarflexion typically intensifies discomfort. Neurologic deficits may include decreased sensation, especially in 2-point discrimination, diminished vibration sense, and limited dorsiflexion, inversion, or eversion. Both dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses should be documented carefully.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
content: Evaluation of chronic exertional compartment syndrome requires a different approach. [10] Patients often report pain that predictably worsens with a specific activity and resolves with rest, and baseline examination usually has normal findings. An exercise challenge, eg, treadmill running or outdoor activity, may be used to reproduce symptoms, followed by immediate reexamination. Once symptomatic, findings may include swelling, muscle herniation, anterior compartment tenderness, pain with passive plantarflexion, and occasionally foot drop.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Evaluation
content: Evaluation and workup of suspected anterior tibial compartment syndrome should be guided primarily by the patient’s history and physical examination, with the diagnosis relying primarily on clinical assessment. The clinical context varies significantly depending on the underlying cause, eg, acute trauma, chronic exertional compartment syndrome, or snake envenomation, and evaluation should focus on identifying the primary etiology of symptoms. In patients presenting with classic signs of compartment syndrome associated with a tibial fracture, additional evaluation is often unnecessary. Laboratory studies performed early in the course typically fall within normal limits.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Evaluation
content: Measurement of intracompartmental pressure remains the gold standard for diagnosing compartment syndrome and is most commonly performed using a needle manometer. Alternative techniques include slit catheters, microtip pressure devices, wick catheters, and microcapillary infusion systems. Ultrasound guidance does not improve the diagnostic accuracy of needle placement. [11] Debate continues regarding absolute pressure cutoffs; in acute compartment syndrome, an absolute pressure greater than 30 mm Hg or a Delta pressure (systolic blood pressure minus compartment pressure) less than 30 mm Hg signals concern. [12]

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Evaluation
content: For chronic exertional compartment syndrome, pressures are measured at rest and then again after the patient exercises until symptom onset. Pressures are compared to baseline values, using the modified Pedowitz criteria, which are widely accepted for diagnosis. The modified Pedowitz criteria are generally accepted for the diagnosis of chronic exertional compartment syndrome, with a positive diagnosis confirmed by the presence of 1 or more of the following findings: Preexercise pressure greater than or equal to 15 mm Hg Postexercise pressure at 1 minute greater than or equal to 30 mm Hg Postexercise pressure at 5 minutes greater than or equal to 25 mm Hg [13] Recent studies have explored noninvasive ultrasound-guided techniques to identify affected individuals. [14]

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Evaluation
content: Imaging studies generally do not contribute to diagnosis but may help exclude other causes of symptoms. Radiographs serve as the initial imaging modality for patients with anterior tibial pain. [15] Emerging technologies, such as infrared spectroscopy and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), may have a future role in diagnosis; however, current evidence does not support their routine use in management.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Treatment / Management
content: The management of anterior leg compartment syndrome depends on the acuity of presentation, the underlying cause, and the presence of objective evidence of compartmental hypertension. The goal in all cases is rapid decompression of elevated intracompartmental pressure to prevent irreversible ischemic injury.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Treatment / Management
content: In acute anterior compartment syndrome, early recognition and prompt surgical intervention are paramount. When the diagnosis is uncertain or the clinical picture does not yet meet diagnostic thresholds, patients may initially be managed conservatively under close observation. Observation is appropriate when the diastolic differential pressure (ΔP), defined as diastolic blood pressure minus intracompartmental pressure, exceeds 30 mm Hg, or when the presentation is not consistent with acute compartment syndrome.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Treatment / Management -- Surgical Decompression
content: Initial management of suspected compartment syndrome includes relieving external compression by bivalving circumferential casts or loosening tight dressings. Splinting the ankle between neutral and approximately 37 degrees of plantar flexion can reduce intracompartmental pressure by optimizing muscle length-tension relationships. Some centers may consider adjunctive hyperbaric oxygen therapy, which enhances the oxygen diffusion gradient across ischemic tissue and can temporarily reduce tissue hypoxia. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy, however, does not replace the need for surgical decompression.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Treatment / Management -- Surgical Decompression
content: Emergent fasciotomy becomes necessary when clinical findings strongly indicate acute compartment syndrome or when compartment pressures approach within 30 mm Hg of the diastolic blood pressure. Delays beyond 6 hours from symptom onset significantly increase the risk of irreversible neuromuscular damage, contracture, and amputation. Intraoperatively, compartment pressures should be compared with preoperative diastolic pressure, as anesthetic agents may transiently lower systemic blood pressure and confound ΔP measurements. Ensuring adequate systemic perfusion before intraoperative assessment remains essential. Late or missed diagnosis generally contraindicates fasciotomy, as decompressing necrotic tissue may precipitate systemic complications, eg, reperfusion injury, myoglobinuria, and sepsis.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Treatment / Management -- Fasciotomy approaches
content: The standard surgical approach involves decompression of all 4 leg compartments through dual medial and lateral incisions. [16] Two vertical skin incisions, each approximately 15 to 18 cm long and separated by an 8 cm skin bridge, provide adequate exposure. The anterolateral incision releases the anterior compartment 1 cm anterior to the intermuscular septum and the lateral compartment 1 cm posterior to it, with careful identification and protection of the superficial peroneal nerve. The posteromedial incision decompresses the superficial and deep posterior compartments, preserving the saphenous vein and nerve while detaching the soleal bridge from the posterior tibia to ensure complete release of the deep posterior compartment. This dual-incision technique allows excellent exposure and decompression but requires 2 wounds, increasing the risk of wound-healing complications.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Treatment / Management -- Fasciotomy approaches
content: An alternative single lateral incision technique may extend from the fibular head to the lateral malleolus. [17] Through this approach, the superficial peroneal nerve is identified and protected, and the anterior and lateral compartments are released as previously described. The superficial posterior compartment is then opened, and the deep posterior compartment is accessed by following the interosseous membrane posteriorly from the fibula and releasing the fascia along this plane. The single-incision approach offers the advantage of 1 wound but provides more limited exposure and places the common peroneal nerve at risk during proximal dissection.
contents: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Treatment / Management -- Fasciotomy approaches. An alternative single lateral incision technique may extend from the fibular head to the lateral malleolus. [17] Through this approach, the superficial peroneal nerve is identified and protected, and the anterior and lateral compartments are released as previously described. The superficial posterior compartment is then opened, and the deep posterior compartment is accessed by following the interosseous membrane posteriorly from the fibula and releasing the fascia along this plane. The single-incision approach offers the advantage of 1 wound but provides more limited exposure and places the common peroneal nerve at risk during proximal dissection.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Treatment / Management -- Management in Special Populations
content: In special populations, the diagnostic and management approach requires modification. In children, clinical assessment is challenging because they may be unable to verbalize pain or paresthesia. When suspicion is high, compartment pressure measurement should be performed under sedation or anesthesia. In patients with coagulopathies, eg, hemophilia, factor VIII replacement should be administered before any invasive pressure monitoring or surgical intervention.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Treatment / Management -- Management of Compartment Syndrome in Traumatic Injuries
content: When the etiology is traumatic, as in tibial fractures, fasciotomy should be combined with fracture stabilization, most commonly open reduction and internal fixation, to restore alignment and prevent recurrent swelling. Plastic surgical consultation is often required for soft tissue coverage, especially when extensive skin necrosis or swelling precludes primary closure.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Treatment / Management -- Chronic Exertional Compartment Syndrome Management
content: In contrast, chronic exertional compartment syndrome is managed along a different paradigm. The initial approach is nonoperative and focuses on activity modification, anti-inflammatory therapy, and rehabilitation. Cessation or reduction of the inciting exercise, combined with stretching, gait retraining, and orthotic correction, is often trialed for 6 to 12 weeks. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy and splinting have no established role in chronic disease. When conservative management fails, elective fasciotomy becomes the treatment of choice. [18] Surgical decompression, performed through open or minimally invasive techniques, has demonstrated symptom relief in up to 70% to 90% of patients, with the majority able to resume their previous activity level. Recurrence may occur in 10% to 20% of cases, usually due to incomplete fascial release or postoperative fibrosis.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnosis of anterior compartment syndrome is broad and includes: Infection, including cellulitis, necrotizing fasciitis, and osteomyelitis Neurologic causes, eg, deep peroneal nerve entrapment Toxicologic causes, including snake envenomation Vascular causes, including deep vein thrombosis, ischemic necrosis or gangrene, and popliteal artery entrapment Trauma, including vascular, nerve, muscle, or fascia soft tissue injuries, and tibia or fibula fractures Musculoskeletal causes (eg, chronic exertional compartment syndrome, stress fractures, and medial tibial stress syndrome) Rhabdomyolysis

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Staging
content: Currently, no staging criteria for acute or chronic compartment syndrome are widely accepted.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis for compartment syndrome depends on the etiology, diagnosis, and time from injury to intervention. If acute compartment syndrome is treated with fasciotomy within 6 hours, complete recovery of limb function is anticipated. After 6 hours of ischemia, necrosis occurs, making 6 hours the accepted upper limit of tissue viability. Fasciotomies of the anterior compartment tend to do better than those of the posterior compartment.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Prognosis
content: Late diagnosis of compartment syndrome leads to irreversible necrosis and subsequently permanent muscle and nerve damage. Patients may develop chronic pain and, in the anterior compartment, deep peroneal nerve palsy and foot drop. Volkmann contracture occurs with myonecrosis and the formation of new fibrous tissue, leading to myotendinous adhesions. This results in a residual deformity and loss of function and can occur in up to 10% of patients with compartment syndrome. Calcific myonecrosis can occur. In chronic exertional compartment syndrome, fasciotomy is associated with high levels of pain relief and patient satisfaction with successful outcomes reported between 80% and 100%.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Complications
content: Infection is a significant complication of compartment syndrome and fasciotomy, with variable rates reported up to 20.8%. Independent risk factors for surgical site infection in this setting include open fractures, elevated body mass index, a history of smoking, and prolonged time to wound closure. [19] [20] Other complications include hematomas and seromas, peripheral nerve injury, and deep vein thrombosis. [21] Complications can be severe, extending to limb amputation and even mortality. [22]

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Complications
content: The recurrence of symptoms ranges from 2% to 17% in published studies, which may be due to incomplete release of the fascial layers, failure to release all of the appropriate compartments, or fascial scarring. Thus, some patients may require revision.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: Postoperative care focuses on effective pain control, as well as prevention of infection and excessive swelling. Patients typically begin ambulation with crutches, which are gradually weaned as weight-bearing tolerance improves. Rehabilitation emphasizes the progressive restoration of hip, knee, and ankle mobility through active and passive range of motion exercises, along with the strengthening of plantarflexion and dorsiflexion. Regular walking is usually achieved within 4 to 6 weeks, while return to running may be possible at approximately 6 weeks. Most patients can expect to achieve full recovery and return to unrestricted activity by around 16 weeks.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Consultations
content: Patients with acute compartment syndrome require consultation with an orthopedic surgeon in the emergency department for immediate surgical fasciotomy. Patients with chronic exertional compartment syndrome can be managed as an outpatient by a sports medicine clinician or orthopedic surgeon.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Preventing anterior tibial compartment syndrome requires careful attention to both medical and surgical practices. Clinicians should ensure that casts, splints, and dressings are applied without excessive tightness, and they should monitor limb positioning during prolonged procedures, eg, the lithotomy position, to reduce external compression. Early recognition and intervention in trauma cases, including prompt stabilization of tibial fractures, can minimize the risk of acute compartment syndrome. Awareness of patient-specific risk factors—such as younger age, open or complex fractures, substance use, and comorbidities like cirrhosis or coagulopathy—supports targeted monitoring. In chronic exertional compartment syndrome, gradual training, activity modification, and appropriate conditioning can reduce the likelihood of repetitive ischemic injury, while vigilance during high-intensity athletic activity allows early detection of concerning symptoms.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Educating patients about anterior tibial compartment syndrome improves early recognition and timely care. Patients should understand the warning signs, eg, pain out of proportion to injury, swelling, tightness, numbness, tingling, and weakness, and report these symptoms promptly. Athletes with chronic exertional compartment syndrome should be advised to monitor for predictable, activity-related pain that resolves with rest and to modify activity or seek medical evaluation if symptoms persist. Postoperative patients and those with casts or splints should receive instructions on monitoring limb circulation, sensation, and mobility, including when to seek immediate medical attention. Clear patient education enhances adherence to care recommendations, facilitates early intervention, and reduces the risk of irreversible tissue damage.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Key factors that should be kept in mind when managing tibial anterior compartment syndrome include: Compartment syndrome represents a mismatch between compartment pressure and arterial blood flow, resulting in tissue ischemia. A traumatic tibial fracture most commonly causes acute compartment syndrome of the anterior leg, although many causes exist. Acute compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency; definitive management is a fasciotomy. Chronic exertional compartment syndrome is an exercise-induced compartment syndrome. Chronic exertional compartment syndrome can be initially managed conservatively, although some cases may require an elective fasciotomy.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Compartment syndrome results from elevated pressure within a closed muscle compartment that impairs tissue perfusion, leading to ischemia and potential irreversible damage to muscles and nerves. The condition most commonly follows acute trauma but may also arise from overuse, vascular events, or iatrogenic causes. The anterior compartment of the leg is most frequently affected, though other extremities may be involved. Acute compartment syndrome constitutes a surgical emergency requiring immediate fasciotomy, while chronic exertional forms are typically managed on an outpatient basis with conservative or elective surgical treatment. Early diagnosis and rapid intervention remain essential to preserve limb function and prevent severe complications.

title: Tibial Anterior Compartment Syndrome -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Effective management of compartment syndrome depends on coordinated teamwork among emergency physicians, orthopedic and plastic surgeons, advanced practitioners, nurses, pharmacists, and physiotherapists. Physicians and advanced practitioners must promptly recognize early symptoms and coordinate urgent surgical consultation. Nurses provide continuous assessment, pain management, and postoperative wound monitoring, while pharmacists ensure safe analgesic and anticoagulant use. Physiotherapists facilitate rehabilitation and functional recovery, and plastic surgeons assist in wound closure and reconstruction. Interprofessional communication, shared decision-making, and timely documentation enhance patient-centered care, improve safety, and reduce morbidity through early intervention, streamlined coordination, and comprehensive recovery planning.
